note.note:
History:
- Presenting complaint: acute chest tightness with wheeze and cough.
- Onset/duration: symptoms began ~3 hours prior to consultation; cough and cold symptoms present for ~1 week (cold last week, runny nose and sore throat improving; cough persisted).
- Symptom progression/context: developed wheeze and increased chest tightness after recent upper respiratory tract infection; mild shortness of breath, worse with exertion (walking up stairs), not short of breath at rest.
- Associated symptoms: non-productive cough, previous sore throat and runny nose; occasional worsening at night. No chest pain reported, sensation of inability to take a full breath.
- Triggers/other: known asthma and allergic rhinitis/hayfever; environmental allergies to dust.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (longstanding; prior severe exacerbation in adolescence requiring hospitalization and intubation at age ~16–17).
- Allergic rhinitis/hayfever; childhood eczema; childhood milk protein allergy.
- Family history: father with asthma; mother with eczema.
- Allergies: no known drug allergies; environmental allergies to dust.
- Current medications: previously used Salbutamol (Ventolin) and inhaled corticosteroid Clenil (Clenil Modulite); patient reports he has run out and does not have inhalers with him currently (conflict noted — see Quality checks).
  - Salbutamol (Ventolin) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Clenil (Clenil Modulite) — dose/route/frequency not documented.

Physical Examination:
- Teleconsultation — no objective vitals or auscultation documented.
- Reported/observed findings:
  - Wheeze reported by patient.
  - Chest tightness; non-productive cough.
  - Not short of breath at rest; increased dyspnea with exertion (stairs).
  - No throat swelling reported.
  - No chest pain; alert and communicative during consultation.

Impression:
- Acute asthma exacerbation with wheeze and chest tightness in the setting of recent upper respiratory tract infection.

Management Plan:
- Prescriptions to be sent:
  - Inhaled medications: Ventolin (Salbutamol) and Clenil (Clenil Modulite) — prescription to be provided (to be sent within approximately 1 hour). Specific inhaler dosing not documented.
  - Spacer to be provided and instructions for use included.
  - Oral corticosteroid prescribed: two tablets in the morning for 5 days; specific steroid name not documented.
- Inhaler use advice:
  - Continue Clenil (inhaled steroid) as maintenance (morning) and use Ventolin as needed for wheeze.
  - Use spacer with inhalers to improve delivery; follow provided instructions (prime with a couple puffs, then inhale, breathe out, repeat for 5–10 breaths as instructed).
- Safety advice & escalation:
  - If using Ventolin more frequently than every 3 hours, seek medical attention.
  - Seek immediate medical care for worsening shortness of breath, increasing chest tightness, chest pain, lightheadedness, or other concerning deterioration.
- Work/activities:
  - Advised to rest; clinician may provide time off work (patient may self-certify for the first seven days).

Patient Summary:
- Patient with known asthma developed wheeze, chest tightness, and non-productive cough after a recent cold; reports being without inhalers for ~1 week. Provider believes this is an asthma exacerbation related to recent upper respiratory infection. Prescriptions for inhaled therapy, a spacer, and a short course of oral steroids will be sent; patient advised on inhaler use and to seek urgent care if symptoms worsen.

Key Takeaways:
- Start prescribed oral steroids (two tablets each morning for 5 days) and restart inhaled steroid (Clenil) daily with Ventolin (Salbutamol) PRN for wheeze.
- Use a spacer with inhalers to improve delivery; follow instructions provided.
- Seek urgent medical attention if Ventolin is needed more often than every 3 hours or if symptoms worsen (increased SOB, chest pain, light-headedness).

Next Steps:
- Patient to obtain and start prescribed inhalers and oral steroid course as sent by clinician.
- Patient to collect spacer and review instructions; begin using spacer with inhalers.
- No routine follow-up scheduled in transcript; patient to seek medical review if symptoms do not improve or if they deteriorate; consider primary care or emergency assessment if frequent reliever use or worsening signs.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: objective vital signs (heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation), peak flow measurement, chest auscultation findings, name and dose of the oral steroid, specific inhaler dosing regimen, smoking status, and documentation of home inhaler possession.
- Internal conflicts from transcript: patient initially states he has run out and does not have inhalers with him; later states "I'm doing pretty good... just on the Clenil and the Salbutamol." Conflict noted regarding current possession/use of inhalers.
- Transcript quality: generally understandable with occasional minor audio dropouts/interruption noted during the consultation.
